options.text: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
The emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus
The absorption of neutrons by a nucleus
The splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei

questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion is the joining (fusing) of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy. This is the process that powers the Sun and all stars.

questions.stem: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures?

options.text: To melt the fuel so it can be poured into the reactor
To remove the electrons from the fuel atoms
To overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nuclei

questions.explanation: Both nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. Extremely high temperatures (millions of degrees) give the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome this electrostatic repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

questions.stem: Where does nuclear fusion occur naturally?

options.text: In the core of stars, including the Sun
In the atmosphere during lightning strikes

questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion occurs naturally in the cores of stars, where temperatures reach millions of degrees and pressure is enormous. In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing the energy that keeps the Sun shining.

questions.stem: What is the main challenge in achieving controlled nuclear fusion on Earth?

options.text: Containing the plasma at temperatures of millions of degrees without it touching the reactor walls

questions.explanation: At the temperatures required for fusion (millions of degrees), matter exists as plasma. No physical material can withstand these temperatures, so the plasma must be contained using magnetic fields, which is extremely difficult.

questions.stem: What state of matter is created at the temperatures needed for fusion?
questions.explanation: At the extreme temperatures required for fusion (millions of degrees), atoms are fully ionised and matter exists as plasma, the fourth state of matter, consisting of free nuclei and electrons.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of fusion over fission as an energy source?

options.text: Fusion fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is abundant and produces little long-lived radioactive waste
Fusion reactors are already commercially available

questions.explanation: Fusion fuel (deuterium from seawater, tritium from lithium) is virtually unlimited, and fusion produces much less long-lived radioactive waste than fission. However, controlled fusion power has not yet been achieved commercially.

questions.stem: In the Sun, what is the main fusion reaction?

options.text: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium

questions.explanation: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei (protons) fuse together through a series of steps to form helium nuclei. This releases enormous amounts of energy, which is the source of the Sun's light and heat.
